header: Three years in, and she still gets sent for the long pole
lead: Lea Wimmer is in the last year of her apprenticeship at Aubruck. We asked her what nobody tells you before you start.
author: Lea Wimmer

questions.title: What did you think the job was, before you started?
questions.bodytext: Standing behind an instrument, mostly. That is about ten per cent of it. The rest is walking, looking for a boundary stone somebody buried under a hedge in 1978, and writing down what you found in a way the next person can use.

questions.title: What was the first week actually like?
questions.bodytext: Cold. I started in February and my first job was the Nauwang sewer re-survey, which is four kilometres of ditch. Milan gave me the pole and said the only wrong thing I could do was hold it crooked and not say so. I held it crooked twice and said so both times.

questions.title: Is there anything you would tell somebody thinking about it?
questions.bodytext: That the maths at college is worse than the maths at work, and that is fine — you get the maths done, and then the work is outside. And that you will be sent for the long pole for about two years. Everyone is. It is not a joke about you, it is that the long pole is heavy and you are the youngest.

questions.title: What surprised you most?
questions.bodytext: How much of it is talking to people. I thought it was a technical job and it is, but half the boundary work is standing in somebody's garden while they explain what their father told them about the fence. You have to be able to listen to that and then measure what is actually there.

questions.title: What happens after the apprenticeship?
questions.bodytext: I stay, if they will have me. Then I want the cadastral qualification, which is another few years of evenings. Andrea has done it and says it is worth it and also that she would not do it again, which I have decided to take as encouragement.
